evidence_quotes.quote: The master-operators are responsible for selling water to consumers, either through piped connections to dwellings or through a network of water kiosks and standpipes for those too poor to afford private connections.

Master-operators ensure that kiosk operators get connected once they have raised enough money to purchase water meters and pipes. In Manyatta B, prospective operators may have to purchase the meter and pipes, and also pay for pipe layout and connection fees. Such requirements prevent those without access to capital from entering the water-service business.

Water prices are set by the master-operators in collaboration with the utility. The utility delivers water in bulk to master-operators at subsidized price. In Manyatta B, kiosk operators set prices opportunistically according to the water situation in the settlement.

In addition, in-depth interviews were conducted with key informants drawn from each of the master operators. Interview questions covered system interactions (management of services, type and frequency, system disruption, revenue collection, sanctions, disconnection frequency).
In Manyatta, 73.3% reported disconnection, compared to 36.2% in Nyalenda A and 23.1% in Nyalenda B.

On average, a 20 l jerrican in Nyalenda A costs 2.97 Ksh; in Nyalenda B it was 2.90 Ksh and 3.70 Ksh in Manyatta B. The lowest price in Nyalenda A and B is Ksh 2.00 same as that of Manyatta; however, the highest price in Manyatta was Ksh 5.00 compared to only Ksh 3.00 in Nyalenda.
Consequently, households that lacked the means to store plenty of clean water continued to rely on cheap and unsafe water whenever kiosk services were interrupted.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines urban drinking-water service access in three informal settlements (slums) in Kisumu, Kenya, focusing on water kiosks and piped networks through which low-income households obtain water.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording: Yes — examines an institutional, regulatory, and governance arrangement, the Delegated Management Model (DMM) utility-community partnership operating under Kenya's Water Act 2002 and WASREB framework. Narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: Yes — directly analyzes concrete rule-type mechanisms governing service access, including utility delegation/contractual structure versus direct utility provision, localized application procedures and connection/start-up fee rules (reducing administrative burden and capital barriers for kiosk operators, especially women), subsidized bulk tariffs and negotiated retail tariff-setting rules, kiosk land-tenure/space rules, and bill-payment enforcement, discretionary temporary accommodation by master operators, and meter disconnection rules.
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary empirical evidence from a comparative mixed-methods study conducted in May-June 2013 across two DMM slums (Nyalenda A and B) and one non-DMM control slum (Manyatta B), using a random sample survey of 103 water-kiosk operators analyzed via percentages and one-way ANOVA, key informant interviews with 8 master operators, and participant observation.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports multiple water-access outcomes: kiosk connection/start-up capital costs, retail water price per 20-L container charged to slum consumers (affordability), operator meter disconnection rates for bill nonpayment, and service disruption/unreliability (meter theft, pipe vandalism, daily disruption complaints, and household fallback to rivers, wells, and springs). Per the 2026-10-14 A18 rule, the finding that reliability had not significantly improved does not affect eligibility.
criterion_notes.c5: Population and unit of analysis (individual water-kiosk operators, N = 103, and master operators, n = 8, serving slum households in Kisumu), exposure (DMM governance, connection, tariff, and disconnection rules vs direct utility provision without DMM), outcomes (start-up/connection cost, retail price per 20-L jerrican, disconnection for nonpayment, and service disruption/reliability), and study design (cross-sectional comparative mixed-methods study) are clearly reported.

study_design: Cross-sectional comparative mixed-methods study (random-sample survey of 103 water-kiosk operators across two DMM slums and one non-DMM control slum analyzed with one-way ANOVA, plus key informant interviews with 8 master operators and participant observation)
population_and_sample: Individual water-kiosk operators (random sample N = 103: Nyalenda A n = 47, Nyalenda B n = 26, Manyatta B n = 30) and master operators (key informants n = 8) providing water services to informal settlement residents in Kisumu city
exposure: Delegated Management Model (DMM) utility-community governance and regulatory structure (bulk metered supply to master operators, localized kiosk application and connection-cost rules, utility-subsidized and negotiated retail tariffs, and collective payment/disconnection enforcement rules) in Nyalenda A and B versus direct utility kiosk connection and management without DMM in Manyatta B
outcome: Kiosk connection/start-up capital costs, retail water price per 20-L container (affordability), meter disconnection due to bill nonpayment, and service reliability/disruption (pipe vandalism, meter theft, daily disruption complaints, and household reliance on unsafe water sources during interruptions)
rationale: This empirical comparative mixed-methods study evaluates how Kisumu's Delegated Management Model (DMM) governs urban slum water service access compared with direct utility kiosk connection in a control slum. It satisfies all inclusion criteria: it examines community/household water service access via shared water kiosks (c1); directly analyzes rule-type institutional and regulatory mechanisms under both the plain and narrow 2026-10-13 readings of Criterion 2, including utility delegation contracts, connection/start-up fee and application rules, subsidized/negotiated tariff rules, and bill-payment enforcement and disconnection rules (c2); provides primary survey and qualitative interview evidence across three settlements (c3); reports concrete access outcomes including connection costs, retail water prices per 20-L jerrican, operator disconnections, and service disruptions (c4); clearly identifies the operator/kiosk unit of analysis, exposure, outcomes, and comparative design (c5); and is written in English (c6).
